_comment_saintDoNotMerge: Merges this project has decided AGAINST, each with the corpus sentence that forbids it. saintMergeVariants above says which names are one person; this says which look like one person and are not. It exists because the merge is the destructive direction: on this corpus the figures most likely to share a name are father and son, uncle and nephew, master and disciple, so a similarity merge does not merely mis-name someone — it deletes the edge that made the pair worth recording. A honorific-stripping token matcher run on 28 August 2026 proposed 21 merges here and 19 were wrong; those 19 are the reason most of these rows exist. Enforced by scripts/data/validate-kg-identity.mjs, which fails the build if any pair collapses into one node and re-checks every quote byte-for-byte against its source. Adding a row is cheap and permanent; deleting one needs a reason better than "the names look the same".

_comment_saintCompositeFigures: Rows whose figure cell names more than one person, mapped to the figures it names, primary first. Applied instead of saintMergeVariants for these cells, and the reason it has to exist: the schema gives a row one `principal_figure`, but some sites are held by two people and the sheet says so — with a `;` in `principal_figure`, and with "&" or "and" in the legacy cell. Every earlier handling lost one of the two. "Guru Nanak and Bhai Mardana" was a saintMergeVariants entry resolving to "Guru Nanak", which is why Bhai Mardana appeared NOWHERE in this graph; the other two became single nodes named after both people, so Gurdwara Panjvi Chati Patshahi reached neither Guru Arjan Dev’s page nor Guru Hargobind’s. The FIRST name listed is the only one the row’s own figure_type / figure_born / figure_died may describe: Rori Sahib records figure_type "Sikh Guru" and Bhai Mardana was not a Guru, so copying it across would make the graph assert what the sheet never said (RULE 2). build-kg.mjs enforces that, logs a `composite-figure-row` review item, and carries the raw cell onto each `buried_at` edge as `asRecorded`. Only add a row here where the cell genuinely names separate people: a `;` inside a parenthetical is not one (darbar-wasif-ali-wasif), nor is one deity under two names ("Jhulelal / Daryalal"), nor a note about practice ("...; veneration of Guru Nanak").
_comment_saintFigureByShrine: Shrine slug -> the figure that site actually commemorates, overriding the row's `Sufi Saint` cell. Needed because the cell-keyed maps above structurally cannot express this: two rows can carry the BYTE-IDENTICAL legacy cell and be about different people, and saintMergeVariants/saintCompositeFigures are keyed on the cell, so anything they do to one they do to both. Use this ONLY where the sheet itself already contradicts the legacy cell (a differing `principal_figure`, `figure_type` or date columns) — never to assert a figure the sheet is silent about (RULE 2). Each entry is a bridge, not a destination: the real fix is a CSV patch correcting the sheet, and `validate-kg-identity.mjs` check 8 fails an entry once the sheet catches up, so a stale override cannot sit here unnoticed.

tomb-of-javindi-bibi.why: The row's `Sufi Saint` cell reads 'Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari' — byte-identical to the cell on 'Shrine of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari', a different monument about a different person — so the graph filed a woman's tomb as one of his two shrines. The sheet already disagrees with itself here in three columns: `principal_figure` is 'Bibi Jawindi', `figure_type` is 'Historical person' where his row says 'Sufi saint', and `figure_born`/`figure_died` (1192/1291) appear only on his row. Nothing is invented by this entry; it adopts what the sheet's own newer columns say. Patch to correct the sheet: data/patch_javindi_bibi_figure_2026-08-28.csv.

_comment_saintDescriptiveCells: Figure cells that are a name PLUS a description, mapped to the name alone. Distinct from saintMergeVariants, which joins spelling variants of one name: these cells are not variants, they are a name with a clause attached — "…, described in the survey as slave of Mahmud Ghaznavi", "…, disciple of Guru Gobind Singh", "…, son of Rama and Sita". slugify() swallowed the clause, so the archive published figure URLs that are whole sentences; malik-ahmad-ayaz's was seventeen words long, and prerender emits a file for each one. The clause is NOT discarded: build-kg keeps the full recorded cell as an altName, so the survey's own wording is still on the figure's page and searchable (RULE 2). Shortening retires a published URL, which retiredSlugs turns into a redirect. Only add a row here where the extra text describes the figure rather than naming them — a longer name is not a description, and 16 of the archive's 21 six-word-plus slugs are simply long names (Shaikh Shihab-ud-Din Abu Hafs Umar al-Suhrawardi) and must be left alone.

_comment_saintDisplayNames: Figure slug -> the name the page should be TITLED with, while the slug itself stays put. Rauf's ruling of 29 August 2026 on the epithet rows: the formal name is the better record and the epithet is what a reader searches for and links to, so the archive keeps both — principal_figure supplies the title, the legacy slug supplies the URL, and the epithet becomes an altName so nothing is lost. This is CLAUDE.md RULE 3 applied literally: a sheet value is a join key and a label is cosmetic, so a better label must never cost a published address. Keyed on the slug rather than on the cell, because the whole point is that the slug does not move. NOT for a row where the two columns name different people, change an honorific class, or turn a person into a collective — three such rows (pir-abdul-ul-karim, guru-gurpat, bibi-pak-daman) were deliberately held out of this ruling and are back in the worksheet unanswered. One thing this quietly fixes: jahaniyan-jahangasht would have become the slug `sayyid-jalaluddin`, one suffix from his grandfather `sayyid-jalaluddin-surkh-posh-bukhari`. Keeping the slug removes the collision that made that row the second place principal_figure was worse. APPLIED TO TWO OF SEVEN so far. The ruling can only be carried out where the formal name exists in URDU: otherwise the English page moves to the formal name and the Urdu page falls back through altNames to the epithet, and the two editions title the same figure differently — which CLAUDE.md's i18n contract forbids and which no gate here would have caught, because the altName fallback keeps the parity test green. Five are waiting on an Urdu name and are listed in _pending_saintDisplayNames; check 9 of validate-kg-identity.mjs fails any entry whose title has no Urdu, so the constraint is now enforced rather than remembered.

_comment_familyRelations: Kinship the archive states in its own prose. 28 edges over 26 rows, every one copied verbatim (name, wording, quote, source) from data/kg-lineage-proposals.json#familyRelations, where an extraction pass recorded them and NOTHING read them: the graph knew only disciple_of and successor_of, so blood and marriage — which is how a gaddi actually passes in this corpus — were held and not rendered. Slugs, kinType and the two role labels are decisions made here by a human; the prose fields are not retyped. Direction is always junior → senior: the subject is the son, grandson, nephew, son-in-law or descendant of the object. `elderRole`/`juniorRole` come from a closed vocabulary because Urdu splits what English does not — a paternal grandfather is دادا and a maternal one نانا — and a label that picks a side the source never states is an invented fact (RULE 2). Where the entry says which line, the specific term is used; where it does not, the *Unspecified role keeps both readings. Two rows in the proposals file record a real family succession and name nobody on the other end; they are in `kinNotes` below, as notes rather than edges, so they are not lost.

_comment_orderProse: What the archive itself says about each of its nine orders, verbatim. Every passage is SLICED out of data/shrines.json by scripts, never retyped, and attributed to the entry it comes from. This exists because the order pages were showing a one-line summary written for this site and nothing else, while the corpus carried whole authored sections on the same orders — "The Suhrawardi Way", "The Way of Blame", "The Azeemia Order", "The Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi Way", "The Qalandar and His Order" — that no page could reach. Same shape as the kinship ties: held and not rendered. Selection rules, learned the hard way: a passage must NAME ITS OWN SUBJECT, because lifted out of its entry a sentence opening on "He" or "Through his disciple" has no antecedent, and the archive’s prose is not ours to patch. Where two entries word the same fact differently, both are kept (see the two Suhrawardi passages) rather than one being silently preferred (RULE 2). Every passage carries `quoteUr`, sliced the same way out of the Urdu article in src/data/urdu-content.json. That is not politeness: an English paragraph standing as the main content of an Urdu order page is an untranslated sentence, which i18n rule 7 forbids and the no-leak guard caught on seven routes the first time this shipped. The archive already held every one of these passages in Urdu — «سلسلہ نقشبندیہ مجددیہ», «ملامت کی راہ», «سلسلہ عظیمیہ» — so the fix was to quote the Urdu article, not to widen the budget.

orderProse.quote: He is counted within the Chishti order, the *silsila* most closely identified with Punjabi and Indian Sufism through its great early masters — Khwaja Mu'in al-Din Chishti of Ajmer and Khwaja Nizam al-Din Awliya of Delhi — and Eidgah Sharif accordingly stands in the Chishti-Nizami current of devotion, with its characteristic emphasis on love of God, service to the poor and the practice of *sama* (spiritual audition).
orderProse.quoteUr: وہ سلسلہ چشتیہ سے تعلق رکھتے ہیں، وہ سلسلہ جو اپنے عظیم ابتدائی مشائخ — اجمیر کے خواجہ معین الدین چشتی اور دہلی کے خواجہ نظام الدین اولیاء — کے ذریعے پنجابی اور ہندوستانی تصوف سے سب سے زیادہ قریبی طور پر پہچانا جاتا ہے، اور عیدگاہ شریف اسی مطابق سلسلہ چشتیہ نظامیہ کے دھارے میں کھڑا ہے، جس کی خصوصی توجہ اللہ کی محبت، غریبوں کی خدمت، اور سماع کی مشق پر ہے۔
orderProse._why: The corpus’s clearest statement of what the Chishti order IS, rather than who belonged to it — masters, current and characteristic practice in one sentence.

orderProse.quote: At Pakpattan, on the old bank of the Sutlej in southern Punjab, stands the shrine of Hazrat Baba Fariduddin Mas‘ud Ganjshakar (c. 1173–1266) — “Baba Farid,” one of the founding saints of the Chishti order in South Asia and among the most beloved holy figures of the Punjab.
orderProse.quoteUr: پاکپتن میں، جنوبی پنجاب میں دریائے ستلج کے پرانے کنارے پر، حضرت بابا فرید الدین مسعود گنج شکر (تقریباً 1173–1266) کا مزار واقع ہے — "بابا فرید"، برصغیر میں سلسلہ چشتیہ کے بانی بزرگوں میں سے ایک اور پنجاب کی سب سے محبوب مقدس ہستیوں میں شمار ہوتے ہیں۔
orderProse._why: Names its own subject. The obvious pick was "the Chishti order he helped root in India became the most widespread of all the Sufi paths of the subcontinent" — a better sentence and an unusable one, because lifted out of its entry it opens on "Through his disciple" with no antecedent. A passage on an order page has to stand alone, and the archive’s prose is not ours to patch.

orderProse.shrineName: Shrine of Abul Faiz Qalander Ali Suharwardi
orderProse.quote: The Suhrawardiyya takes its name from Abu Najib al-Suhrawardi and, above all, from his nephew Shaikh Shihab al-Din Umar al-Suhrawardi of Baghdad, whose manual *‘Awarif al-Ma‘arif* became one of the classic guides of the Sufi path. In contrast to some of the more antinomian and ecstatic movements, the Suhrawardi way was known for its sobriety, its insistence on the outward law and on refined manners (*adab*), and its readiness to engage with rulers and society for the good of the community — a temper well suited to a scholar-saint.
orderProse.quoteUr: سہروردیہ اپنا نام ابو نجیب سہروردی سے، اور سب سے بڑھ کر ان کے بھتیجے شیخ شہاب الدین عمر سہروردی بغدادی سے لیتا ہے، جن کی کتاب عوارف المعارف صوفی راہ کی کلاسیکی رہنما کتابوں میں سے ایک بن گئی۔ کچھ زیادہ آزاد اور وجدانی تحریکوں کے برخلاف، سہروردی راہ اپنی سنجیدگی، شریعت اور نفیس آداب پر اصرار، اور برادری کی بھلائی کے لیے حکمرانوں اور معاشرے سے تعامل کی تیاری کے لیے جانی جاتی تھی — ایک ایسا مزاج جو ایک عالم بزرگ کے لیے موزوں تھا۔
orderProse._why: From the archive’s own section "The Suhrawardi Way": the order’s name, its founding texts and its temper.

orderProse.quote: The Suhrawardi order he founded was marked by strict adherence to the Sharia, sober devotion, learning, and an active engagement with society and state — a pattern that made Multan a hub of both spiritual authority and worldly influence, and that shaped the religious life of the western Punjab and Sindh for centuries.
orderProse.quoteUr: ان کا قائم کردہ سہروردی سلسلہ شریعت کی سخت پابندی، متوازن عبادت، علم، اور معاشرے و ریاست سے فعال رابطے سے ممتاز تھا — ایک ایسا انداز جس نے ملتان کو روحانی اقتدار اور دنیاوی اثر دونوں کا مرکز بنایا، اور جس نے صدیوں تک مغربی پنجاب اور سندھ کی مذہبی زندگی کو تشکیل دیا۔
orderProse._why: Kept beside the passage above ON PURPOSE, and not reconciled with it. This entry says Zakariya "founded" the order; the Abul Faiz entry says the Suhrawardiyya takes its name from Abu Najib and Shihab al-Din of Baghdad and "was carried into the Indian subcontinent" by Zakariya. Two entries of this archive word the same relationship differently, and showing both is the archive reporting what it holds rather than picking a winner (RULE 2).

orderProse.quote: Shams Ali Qalandar stood in the tradition of the *qalandars* — the wandering, often unconventional Sufi ascetics who, from medieval times, chose a path of renunciation and ecstatic devotion that set them apart from the more sober, respectable orders. In the reckoning of his followers he belonged to the *Owaisi Qadiriyya Noshahi* lineage, a branch of the great *Qadiri* order (traced to the twelfth-century saint Abd al-Qadir Jilani of Baghdad) as transmitted through the Noshahi Sufis of the Punjab; the epithet *Owaisi* denotes, in Sufi usage, a spiritual initiation received inwardly rather than from a living master, in the manner of the early devotee Uways al-Qarani.
orderProse.quoteUr: شمس علی قلندر قلندروں کی روایت میں کھڑے تھے — وہ گھومنے پھرنے والے، اکثر غیر روایتی صوفی زاہد جنہوں نے، قرون وسطیٰ سے، ترک دنیا اور وجدانی عقیدت کی ایک ایسی راہ چنی جو انہیں زیادہ سنجیدہ، قابل احترام سلسلوں سے الگ کرتی تھی۔ ان کے پیروکاروں کے حساب سے وہ اویسی قادریہ نوشاہی سلسلے سے تعلق رکھتے تھے، سلسلہ قادریہ کی ایک شاخ (جو بغداد کے بارہویں صدی کے بزرگ عبدالقادر جیلانی تک جاتی ہے) جو پنجاب کے نوشاہی صوفیوں کے ذریعے منتقل ہوئی؛ لقب "اویسی" صوفی استعمال میں ایک ایسی روحانی بیعت کی نشاندہی کرتا ہے جو کسی زندہ مرشد کی بجائے باطنی طور پر حاصل کی جاتی ہے، ابتدائی معتقد اویس قرنی کے انداز میں۔
orderProse._why: Carries the order’s eponym and date, and defines *Owaisi* — which is also the standing reason no person-to-person lineage edge may be drawn for this figure. Its first sentence is also the Qalandariyya’s passage, deliberately: the same paragraph places this figure in both traditions, which is why the archive records him under both.

orderProse.quote: At Shergarh, in the Okara district of the Punjab, stands the shrine of Hazrat Daud Bandagi Kirmani (1513–1575) — a revered Qadiri saint of the sixteenth century who did much to spread the Qadiri order in the Punjab.
orderProse.quoteUr: شیرگڑھ میں، پنجاب کے ضلع اوکاڑہ میں، حضرت داؤد بندگی کرمانی (1513–1575) کا مزار واقع ہے — سولہویں صدی کے معزز قادری بزرگ جنہوں نے پنجاب میں سلسلہ قادریہ کے پھیلاؤ میں بہت کچھ کیا۔
orderProse._why: How the order reached the Punjab, from the entry of a saint who carried it there — and a sentence that names him, which "From his base at Shergarh he taught" does not.

orderProse.quote: Shams Ali Qalandar stood in the tradition of the *qalandars* — the wandering, often unconventional Sufi ascetics who, from medieval times, chose a path of renunciation and ecstatic devotion that set them apart from the more sober, respectable orders.
orderProse.quoteUr: شمس علی قلندر قلندروں کی روایت میں کھڑے تھے — وہ گھومنے پھرنے والے، اکثر غیر روایتی صوفی زاہد جنہوں نے، قرون وسطیٰ سے، ترک دنیا اور وجدانی عقیدت کی ایک ایسی راہ چنی جو انہیں زیادہ سنجیدہ، قابل احترام سلسلوں سے الگ کرتی تھی۔
orderProse._why: The archive’s own section "The Qalandar and His Order", and the only passage in the corpus that defines the qalandari way as such.

orderProse.shrineName: Shrine of Ganj e Inayat Sarkar
orderProse.quote: The Naqshbandiyya takes its name from Khwaja Baha-ud-Din Naqshband of Bukhara (d. 1389), and is distinguished among the Sufi paths by its preference for the silent, hidden remembrance of God (*dhikr-e-khafi*) over audible or ecstatic forms, and by its insistence that the mystical life be lived in strict conformity with the Sharia and in the midst of society rather than in withdrawal from it — expressed in the famous Naqshbandi principle of “solitude within the crowd.” The order was carried into India around 1600 by Khwaja Baqi Billah, and it was his disciple Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi — revered as the *Mujaddid Alf-e-Sani*, the “Renewer of the Second Millennium” — who reshaped it into the Mujaddidi branch, laying a powerful stress on the purification of belief, the reaffirmation of God’s absolute oneness, and the reform of practice in accordance with the Prophet’s example. From Sirhindi’s Sirhind the Mujaddidi way spread across the subcontinent and beyond, becoming one of the great engines of Islamic renewal in South Asia.
orderProse.quoteUr: نقشبندیہ اپنا نام بخارا کے خواجہ بہاؤالدین نقشبند (وفات 1389) سے لیتا ہے، اور صوفی راستوں میں اپنی خاموش، پوشیدہ ذکر (ذکر خفی) کو باآواز یا وجدانی صورتوں پر ترجیح دینے، اور اس اصرار کے لیے ممتاز ہے کہ صوفیانہ زندگی شریعت کی سخت پابندی کے ساتھ اور معاشرے سے کنارہ کشی کے بجائے اس کے درمیان گزاری جائے — جسے مشہور نقشبندی اصول "خلوت در انجمن" میں بیان کیا جاتا ہے۔ یہ سلسلہ تقریباً 1600 میں خواجہ باقی باللہ کے ذریعے ہندوستان لایا گیا، اور ان کے مرید شیخ احمد سرہندی — جنہیں مجدد الف ثانی، "دوسرے ہزار سال کے مجدد"، کے طور پر عزت دی جاتی ہے — نے اسے مجددی شاخ میں ڈھالا، عقیدے کی پاکیزگی، اللہ کی مطلق وحدانیت کی توثیق، اور رسول اللہ کی سیرت کے مطابق عمل کی اصلاح پر زبردست زور دیتے ہوئے۔ سرہند سے مجددی راہ برصغیر اور اس سے آگے پھیلی، جنوبی ایشیا میں اسلامی تجدید کے عظیم انجنوں میں سے ایک بن کر۔
orderProse._why: From the archive’s section "The Naqshbandi-Mujaddidi Way". Covers the eponym, silent dhikr, "solitude within the crowd", and the Mujaddidi branch — which is the branch 2 of the 10 memberships actually name.

orderProse.shrineName: Dargah of Pir Muhammad Rashid (Roze Dhani), Pir Jo Goth
orderProse.quote: The town of Pir Jo Goth — "the village of the Pir" — in the Kingri taluka of Khairpur District, Sindh, grew up around the shrine of Pir Syed Muhammad Rashid Shah (1757–1818), known by his honorific Roze Dhani, "master of the shrine," the founder of the Rashidi Sufi order and an ancestor of the line of Pir Pagara.
orderProse.quoteUr: قصبہ پیر جو گوٹھ — "پیر کا گاؤں" — سندھ کے ضلع خیرپور کی کنگری تعلقہ میں، پیر سیّد محمد راشد شاہ (1757–1818) کے مزار کے گرد پروان چڑھا، جو اپنے اعزازی لقب "روزے دھنی" یعنی "مزار کے مالک" سے معروف ہیں، سلسلہ راشدیہ کے بانی اور پیر پگارا کے سلسلے کے جدِ امجد۔
orderProse._why: The order had NO description at all. This is the corpus naming its founder, its date and its descent — and it is the sentence the seed’s taxonomy note was already quoting where no reader could see it.

orderProse.shrineName: Dargah of Pir Muhammad Rashid (Roze Dhani), Pir Jo Goth
orderProse.quote: The dargah is distinguished by an austere discipline unusual among Sufi shrines: devotees are required to enter only with the head covered, the Hur faqirs make pilgrimage at fixed times of the year, and the sacred date of 27 Rajab draws great throngs of mureeds — yet, in contrast to the festive urs kept at most Sufi tombs, the Rashidi tradition is said to observe no public urs here.
orderProse.quoteUr: دربار صوفی مزارات میں ایک غیر معمولی سخت نظم و ضبط سے ممتاز ہے: عقیدت مندوں کے لیے صرف سر ڈھانپ کر داخل ہونا لازم ہے، حُر فقیر سال کے مقررہ اوقات میں زیارت کرتے ہیں، اور 27 رجب کی مقدس تاریخ مریدوں کے بڑے مجمعے کھینچتی ہے — پھر بھی، بیشتر صوفی مزارات پر منائے جانے والے پُرمسرت عرس کے برعکس، کہا جاتا ہے کہ راشدی روایت یہاں کوئی عوامی عرس نہیں مناتی۔
orderProse._why: A practice of the order stated as a practice, and one that contradicts the archive’s own default assumption that a Sufi shrine keeps an urs.

orderProse.shrineName: Shrine of Hazrat Madho Lal Hussain (Shah Hussain Darbar)
orderProse.quote: Hussain belonged, in spirit, to the *Malamatiyya* — the Sufis of the “path of blame,” who deliberately drew the censure of respectable society upon themselves in order to kill the ego’s hunger for esteem, hiding their inner sanctity beneath an outward show of impropriety.
orderProse.quoteUr: حسین روح کے اعتبار سے ملامتیہ سے تعلق رکھتے تھے — "راہِ ملامت" کے صوفی، جو جان بوجھ کر باعزت معاشرے کی ملامت اپنے اوپر کھینچتے تھے تاکہ عزت کی انا کی بھوک کو مار سکیں، اپنی باطنی تقدس کو بے حیائی کے ظاہری مظاہرے کے نیچے چھپاتے ہوئے۔
orderProse._why: The archive’s section "The Way of Blame". The order had no description; this is the definition the corpus already held.

orderProse.quote: Qalandar Baba Auliya’s lasting legacy is the Azeemia Sufi order, which he founded and which was carried on and spread by his foremost disciple, Khwaja Shamsuddin Azeemi. The order is distinctive for its emphasis on the systematic teaching of Sufi inner science — meditation, spiritual healing, and the understanding of consciousness — presented in a modern idiom, and it has established centres in Pakistan and among the diaspora. The shrine in Karachi is the spiritual centre of this living movement, a place of both devotion and study.
orderProse.quoteUr: قلندر بابا اولیاء کا پائیدار ورثہ سلسلہ عظیمیہ ہے، جسے انہوں نے قائم کیا اور جسے ان کے سب سے بڑے مرید، خواجہ شمس الدین عظیمی نے آگے بڑھایا اور پھیلایا۔ یہ سلسلہ تصوف کے باطنی علم — مراقبہ، روحانی شفا، اور شعور کی تفہیم — کی منظم تعلیم پر زور دینے کی وجہ سے ممتاز ہے، جسے ایک جدید اسلوب میں پیش کیا جاتا ہے، اور اس نے پاکستان اور بیرون ملک مقیم پاکستانیوں میں مراکز قائم کیے ہیں۔ کراچی میں مزار اس زندہ تحریک کا روحانی مرکز ہے، ایک ایسی جگہ جو عقیدت اور علم دونوں کی حامل ہے۔
orderProse._why: The archive’s section "The Azeemia Order" in full — founder, successor, teaching and seat. A twentieth-century order the archive documents well and the order page showed nothing of.

orderProse.quote: Born around 1643 in Kasur into a farming family of the Arain community, Shah Inayat trained under a Shattari Sufi teacher — named in earlier sourcing for this entry as Muhammad Ali Raza Shattari, and named in a 2026 field survey as Hazrat Shah Raza Qadri Shattari; the two names are close but not identical, and neither source has been checked against the other here, so both are recorded rather than one being silently preferred.
orderProse.quoteUr: تقریباً 1643 میں قصور میں آرائیں برادری کے ایک کاشتکار خاندان میں پیدا ہوئے، شاہ عنایت نے ایک شطاری صوفی استاد سے تربیت پائی — اِس اندراج کے پہلے ماخذ میں اُن کا نام محمد علی رضا شطاری بتایا گیا ہے، اور 2026 کے ایک فیلڈ سروے میں حضرت شاہ رضا قادری شطاری؛ دونوں نام قریب ہیں مگر ایک نہیں، اور یہاں کسی ایک ماخذ کو دوسرے کے مقابل جانچا نہیں گیا، لہٰذا دونوں درج کیے جا رہے ہیں بجائے اِس کے کہ خاموشی سے ایک کو ترجیح دی جائے۔
orderProse._why: Two quotations from one entry rather than one long one. The obvious span — first sentence to last — swept in a paragraph about friction with Kasur’s ruling family that has nothing to do with the silsila, and cutting the middle out of a quotation is not something this archive does. So the two sentences that ARE about the Shattari are quoted separately and in order. The thinnest of the nine, and left thin. This is the whole of what the corpus says about the Shattari as a silsila: that one man trained under a Shattari teacher and held the two silsilas together in his practice. Started a sentence earlier than the obvious one so the passage names him — and so it carries the archive’s own refusal to choose between two sources that name that teacher differently. Nothing here defines the order, and nothing pretends to.

orderProse.quote: He combined the Qadiri and Shattari silsilas in his own practice and authored several Persian works of mystical philosophy, including the *Dastur-ul-Amal* (also independently named in the field survey) and *Lata'if-e-Ghaibiya*.
orderProse.quoteUr: اُنہوں نے اپنی مشق میں سلسلہ قادریہ اور شطاریہ کو یکجا کیا اور عرفانی فلسفے پر کئی فارسی تصانیف لکھیں، جن میں *دستورالعمل* (جس کا نام فیلڈ سروے میں بھی آزادانہ طور پر آیا ہے) اور *لطائفِ غیبیہ* شامل ہیں۔
orderProse._why: The other half. Opens on "He", which a passage on an order page normally may not — allowed here only because it follows the passage above it, from the same entry, which names him two lines up.

orderProse.quote: Well educated in Arabic and Persian and in the religious sciences, Bulleh Shah might have become a scholar of the orthodox kind — but he was drawn instead to the burning inward path, and became the disciple of Shah Inayat Qadiri, a Sufi master of Lahore of the Qadiri-Shattari line, who was by trade an *arain* (a gardener-cultivator) rather than a high-born sayyid.
orderProse.quoteUr: عربی، فارسی اور دینی علوم میں خوب تعلیم یافتہ، بلھے شاہ ایک روایتی عالم بن سکتے تھے — مگر وہ اس کے بجائے سلگتی ہوئی باطنی راہ کی طرف کھنچے، اور لاہور کے ایک صوفی مرشد شاہ عنایت قادری کے مرید بنے، جو قادری شطاری سلسلے سے تھے اور جو پیشے کے اعتبار سے ایک اعلیٰ نسب سیّد کے بجائے ایک "اراٴیں" (کاشتکار باغبان) تھے۔
orderProse._why: The second and last mention: the same man named from his disciple’s entry as "of the Qadiri-Shattari line".

_comment_saintOrders: Hand-authored figure → order memberships. Keys must match the slug generated from the canonical saint name after merge variants are applied. THESE ARE UNSOURCED BY CONSTRUCTION — there is no quote field — and on 29 August 2026 an audit against the sheet found two of the six that could be checked were simply wrong, and wrong in the same way: Daud Bandagi Kirmani was seeded chishtiyya where his row's silsila cell says "Qadiri" and his entry calls him "a revered Qadiri saint" who "became a shaykh of the Qadiri order"; Waris Shah was seeded qadiriyya where his cell says "Chishti" and his entry says he "belonged in spirit to the Chishti Sufi tradition". A straight transposition. Nothing in the archive supported either seeded value, and because these edges carry method:"human" the UI showed the wrong one WITHOUT the unreviewed chip that the correct machine-extracted edge beside it carried. Both corrected to the sheet. The invariant is now enforced: a hand-seeded order that does not match the figure's own silsila cell must be declared in saintOrdersNotInCell with a reason, or the build fails.
_comment_saintOrdersNotInCell: Hand-seeded memberships that deliberately do NOT match the figure's own silsila cell. A mismatch is an error unless it is recorded here with the evidence for it — that is the whole point of the list.

saintOrdersNotInCell.reason: Both readings are the archive's own and neither replaces the other. The silsila cell records his initiatic line, and the graph carries that edge too (qadiriyya, from the cell). The qalandariyya edge records what the entry's own section "The Qalandar and His Order" says he WAS. A figure can stand in a tradition and be initiated in a silsila, and this archive reports both rather than choosing.
saintOrdersNotInCell.quote: Shams Ali Qalandar stood in the tradition of the *qalandars* — the wandering, often unconventional Sufi ascetics who, from medieval times, chose a path of renunciation and ecstatic devotion that set them apart from the more sober, respectable orders.

traditions.name: Nath
traditions.definition: The Naths, who flourished across northern India, Nepal, and the north-western frontier from roughly the early medieval centuries, practised a rigorous discipline of yoga and *hatha* austerity and revered Shiva as the *adi-nath*, the first lord and archetypal yogi.
traditions.definitionUr: ناتھ، جو قرون وسطیٰ کے ابتدائی صدیوں سے شمالی ہندوستان، نیپال، اور شمال مغربی سرحد بھر میں پروان چڑھے، یوگا اور ہٹھ ریاضت کا ایک سخت نظم و ضبط اپناتے تھے اور شیو کو آدی ناتھ، پہلا آقا اور نمونہ یوگی، کے طور پر پوجتے تھے۔

traditions.name: Udasi
traditions.definition: The distinctive character of Sadh Belo flows from its rootedness in the *Udasipanth*. This religious and ascetic movement grew from the teachings of Sri Chand, the elder son of Guru Nanak, and blended devotional streams in a manner that resists neat sectarian classification, honouring Sikh scripture and Hindu deities alike, and cultivating a tradition of renunciation, pilgrimage and hospitality.
traditions.definitionUr: سادھ بیلو کا منفرد کردار اس کے "اداسی پنتھ" میں جڑ پکڑنے سے پھوٹتا ہے۔ یہ مذہبی اور سنیاسی تحریک گرو نانک کے بڑے بیٹے سری چند کی تعلیمات سے پروان چڑھی، اور اس نے عقیدتی دھاروں کو ایسے انداز میں ملایا جو کسی صاف ستھری فرقہ وارانہ درجہ بندی میں نہیں آتا، سکھ صحیفے اور ہندو دیوتاؤں دونوں کا احترام کرتی، اور ترک، زیارت اور مہمان نوازی کی روایت پروان چڑھاتی ہے۔

traditions.name: Pranami
traditions.definition: The Pranami *sampradaya* — also called *Dhami* or *Nijananda* — is a Vaishnava tradition within Hinduism centred on the worship of *Krishna*. It emerged in western India in the seventeenth century from the teachings of the *bhakti* saint Devchandra Maharaj and, above all, of his foremost disciple Mehraj Thakur, better known as *Mahamati Prannath*, from whose name the tradition takes its own. Its adherents "bow" (*pranam*) in devotion — hence the name Pranami — and its teaching, gathered in a scripture called the *Tartam Sagar*, is notable for a strongly monotheistic emphasis and for language that sought common ground between Hindu and Islamic conceptions of the divine.
traditions.definitionUr: پرنامی سمپردایہ — جسے دھامی یا نجانند بھی کہا جاتا ہے — ہندومت کے اندر ایک وشنو روایت ہے جو کرشن کی پوجا پر مرکوز ہے۔ یہ سترہویں صدی میں مغربی ہندوستان میں بھکتی بزرگ دیوچندر مہاراج، اور سب سے بڑھ کر، ان کے سب سے بڑے شاگرد مہراج ٹھاکر، جو مہاماتی پرن ناتھ کے نام سے زیادہ معروف ہیں، کی تعلیمات سے ابھرا، جن کے نام سے یہ روایت اپنا نام لیتی ہے۔ اس کے پیروکار عقیدت میں "پرنام" کرتے ہیں — اسی سے پرنامی نام آیا — اور اس کی تعلیم، تارتم ساگر نامی صحیفے میں جمع، ایک زبردست توحیدی زور اور ایسی زبان کے لیے قابل ذکر ہے جو الٰہی کے ہندو اور اسلامی تصورات کے درمیان مشترکہ زمین تلاش کرتی تھی۔

traditions.name: Swaminarayan
traditions.definition: The Swaminarayan movement takes its name from *Swaminarayan* (Sahajanand Swami, 1781–1830), the reformer and teacher who gathered a large following across Gujarat and Kutch and preached a disciplined, devotional Hinduism centred on the worship of Narayana, ethical conduct, and service.
traditions.definitionUr: سوامی نارائن تحریک اپنا نام سوامی نارائن (سہجانند سوامی، 1781–1830) سے لیتی ہے، وہ مصلح اور استاد جنہوں نے گجرات اور کچھ بھر میں ایک وسیع پیروکاری جمع کی اور نارائن کی پوجا، اخلاقی طرز عمل، اور خدمت پر مرکوز ایک منظم، عقیدت مندانہ ہندومت کی تبلیغ کی۔

traditions.name: Daduvansi
traditions.definition: Local tradition associates the shrine with a *sant* named Bhagat Ram, remembered as one of a line of Hindu holy men active in and around Dadu, sometimes described as belonging to a *Daduvansi* lineage — literally the "line" or descendants of a saintly founder.
traditions.definitionUr: مقامی روایت مزار کو بھگت رام نامی ایک سنت سے جوڑتی ہے، جنہیں دادو اور اس کے گرد و نواح میں فعال ہندو بزرگوں کے ایک سلسلے میں سے ایک کے طور پر یاد کیا جاتا ہے، بعض اوقات ایک "دادووَنسی" سلسلے سے تعلق رکھنے والے کے طور پر بیان کیا جاتا ہے — لفظی طور پر ایک متبرک بانی کی "لائن" یا اولاد۔

traditions.name: Shakti Peetha
traditions.definition: The sanctity of Hinglaj is rooted in the pan-Indian legend of the *Shakti Peethas*. According to tradition, the goddess Sati, wife of Shiva, immolated herself in grief and outrage when her father Daksha insulted her husband. The bereaved Shiva, cradling her corpse, began the cosmic dance of destruction, the *tandava*, threatening the universe itself. To end his frenzy, Vishnu released his discus, the *Sudarshana Chakra*, which dismembered Sati's body; wherever a part fell to earth, a *Shakti Peetha* arose, charged with the presence of the goddess.
traditions.definitionUr: ہنگلاج کی تقدس شکتی پیٹھوں کی عالمگیر ہندوستانی روایت میں جڑی ہے۔ روایت کے مطابق، شیو کی اہلیہ دیوی ستی نے اُس وقت غم و غضب میں خود کو آگ کے حوالے کر دیا جب ان کے والد دکش نے ان کے شوہر کی توہین کی۔ سوگوار شیو نے ان کی نعش کو اٹھائے ہوئے تباہی کا کائناتی رقص "تانڈو" شروع کر دیا، جس سے خود کائنات کو خطرہ لاحق ہو گیا۔ ان کے جنون کو ختم کرنے کے لیے وشنو نے اپنا چکر "سدرشن چکر" چلایا، جس نے ستی کے جسم کے ٹکڑے کر دیے؛ جہاں جہاں کوئی حصہ زمین پر گرا، وہاں ایک شکتی پیٹھ وجود میں آیا، جو دیوی کی موجودگی سے معمور ہوا۔

traditionMemberships.quote: The temple's saint, Ratan Nath, belongs to the *Nath sampradaya*, the order of *kanphata* ("split-eared") yogis who trace their lineage to Gorakhnath and, before him, to Matsyendranath, the semi-legendary founder of the sect.

The temple honours Guru Gorakhnath, one of the most influential figures of medieval Indian spirituality, traditionally held to have lived somewhere between the ninth and twelfth centuries CE and revered as a *mahasiddha* and the founder of the *Nath* order of *yogis*.

It became the principal seat of the *Kanphata* yogis — the "split-eared" ascetics, so called from the great rings inserted through the cartilage of their ears at initiation — an order that looked to Gorakhnath as its master.

One of the most important living centres of Hindu worship in the province, it is intimately bound to the *Udasi* tradition, the ascetic order that traces its lineage to Sri Chand, elder son of Guru Nanak
The darbar belongs to the shared Nanakpanthi and *Udasi* devotional world of Sindh, in which Sindhi Hindus and Sikhs venerated the Gurus together.

At Malka Hans, a historic village of the Pakpattan district in southern Punjab, stands the crumbling but still imposing *Parnami* (or *Pranami*) temple, one of the most significant surviving monuments of a distinctive Hindu devotional tradition in Pakistan.

Jinnah Road in the heart of Karachi, is the principal Hindu temple of Pakistan's largest city and the only surviving temple of the *Swaminarayan Sampradaya* — the devotional tradition founded in early nineteenth-century Gujarat — in the country.

traditionMemberships.shrineName: Sant Baba Bhagat Ram Darbar Mandir
traditionMemberships.quote: Local tradition associates the shrine with a *sant* named Bhagat Ram, remembered as one of a line of Hindu holy men active in and around Dadu, sometimes described as belonging to a *Daduvansi* lineage — literally the "line" or descendants of a saintly founder.
It is one of the fifty-one *Shakti Peethas* venerated across the subcontinent, and one of only two situated in present-day Pakistan.
Simultaneously a temple, a fabled university, and one of the great *Shakti Peethas*, Sharada Peeth occupies a singular place in the cultural and religious memory of Kashmir.
